text: What is the rarest material in the universe?

It depends how you measure rarity. First, by abundance. About three quarters of ordinary matter is hydrogen, and about a quarter is helium. Everything heavier adds up to roughly two percent. And ordinary matter itself is only about five percent of the universe's energy content.

Where do the heavy elements come from? The Big Bang made hydrogen and helium. Stars fuse elements up to iron. Beyond iron, some form slowly in aging stars, and others in violent events. In two thousand seventeen, astronomers watched two neutron stars merge, and saw signs of heavy elements being made. How much of our gold came from mergers is still being worked out. A twenty twenty five study says giant magnetar flares may add up to a tenth.

In Earth's crust, gold is about four parts per billion, and platinum about five. The rarest natural element there is astatine. Estimates run from under one gram to about twenty eight grams in the whole crust, because even its longest lived form lasts only about eight hours.

Now measure a different way: by where a material occurs. Some materials need life. Wood is cellulose and lignin, made by land plants. Much limestone is made from the shells of living things. Coal is fossil plants. As far as we know, all of these exist on one planet only: Earth.
Take wood. The oldest known forests are about three hundred eighty six million years old, found in New York. Before land plants grew tall, there was no wood.

But we have looked at very little. Spacecraft have visited a handful of worlds. NASA has confirmed more than six thousand planets around other stars, and we know almost nothing about their surfaces. So wood is rare in the only place we have looked closely. That tells us about our sample. It is not a law of nature.
So what is rarest? By abundance, astatine in Earth's crust. By place, materials that need life, so far. Rarity depends on how you ask.
